title: Kotlin Multiplatform
scopeHtml: Scope: what KMP shares and what it should not, expect/actual, source sets, KMP libraries and DI, Compose Multiplatform status, iOS interop, shared-module architecture, testing, Gradle pitfalls, adoption trade-offs and KMP vs Flutter/React Native. Version notes come from kotlinlang.org and developer.android.com/kotlin/multiplatform as read in Nov 2026; anything else is marked "verify".

questions.promptHtml: What does Kotlin Multiplatform actually share between Android and iOS, and what should you deliberately not share?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who say "KMP shares everything" have never shipped it. The signal is whether you know the share/native boundary and why it exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: KMP compiles one Kotlin codebase to JVM bytecode for Android and to a native binary (via LLVM) for iOS. I share logic that has no platform dependency: networking, serialization, caching, domain rules, validation, state holders. I keep platform-specific things native or behind interfaces: permissions, push, camera, background scheduling, accessibility, and often the UI itself. Sharing is opt-in per module, so you pick the boundary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
KMP is not a runtime or a UI toolkit. It is a compilation model: commonMain code is compiled once per target. Android gets normal bytecode. iOS gets a Kotlin/Native framework (an Objective-C-visible .framework) that Xcode links. There is no bridge or VM at runtime on iOS, which is why performance is native-class.

              commonMain (pure Kotlin + KMP libs)
              /                              \
        androidMain                        iosMain
   (Context, WorkManager,             (Foundation, UIKit,
    Keystore, Play APIs)               Keychain, BGTaskScheduler)

Good candidates to share, ranked by return: (1) API client + DTO + mappers, (2) domain/use cases/business rules (pricing, validation, sync conflict logic), (3) local persistence schema and queries, (4) presentation state holders, (5) UI (only via Compose Multiplatform, a separate decision, see Q305). Poor candidates: anything whose behavior must match the OS feel (navigation transitions, text input, share sheets), anything where a platform SDK is the product (payments SDKs, camera pipelines, maps), and code a platform team will change weekly on its own schedule. The rule I use: share where divergence is a bug (two implementations of a tax rule), not where divergence is the point (a native date picker).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain: shared rule, divergence here would be a bug
class DiscountPolicy {
    fun apply(subtotalPaise: Long, tier: Tier): Long =
        when (tier) { Tier.GOLD -> subtotalPaise * 90 / 100; else -> subtotalPaise }
}
enum class Tier { GOLD, BASIC }

// NOT shared: platform capability hidden behind an interface
interface BiometricGate { suspend fun authenticate(): Boolean }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sharing UI "because we can" before the team has the Compose-on-iOS operational story.
  • Sharing code that depends on the Android Context and then patching with expect/actual everywhere.
  • Treating the share percentage as a success metric instead of defect and delivery-time deltas.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is there a runtime like React Native's bridge? → No. iOS gets a native binary; the interop cost is at the ObjC/Swift API surface, not at runtime.
  2. Can an iOS-only team consume it without Kotlin knowledge? → Yes as a framework/XCFramework (or SPM binary target), but they will debug Kotlin stack traces eventually.
  3. Where does sharing hurt? → Release coupling: a shared module change must be validated on both platforms, so test and CI ownership must be joint.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "business logic and networking". Senior: names a decision rule (divergence is a bug vs the point), mentions release coupling and ownership, and treats UI sharing as a separate, reversible decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that shared a "common" module of 60 percent of the codebase including navigation glue often rolled part of it back when platform teams could not ship independently.

questions.promptHtml: How do expect/actual declarations work, and when would you prefer an interface instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first KMP-specific language feature. Seniors know its limits and the recommended alternative.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: expect declares a signature in common code with no implementation. Each platform source set supplies an actual with the same name and package. The compiler checks every target has one. For anything non-trivial I prefer a plain interface in common code plus a platform implementation injected via DI, because it is mockable, allows several implementations, and avoids the Beta status of expect/actual classes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules from the Kotlin docs: the expect declaration contains no implementation; the actual lives in the same package; every platform source set (or an intermediate one like iosMain covering all iOS targets) must provide it. Works on functions, properties, objects, classes, interfaces, enums, annotations. Actual typealias can map an expect class to an existing platform type (actual typealias Month = java.time.Month). Expected/actual classes are Beta and need -Xexpect-actual-classes; the docs themselves recommend interface + factory function instead.

commonMain:  expect fun platformName(): String
androidMain: actual fun platformName() = "Android ${Build.VERSION.SDK_INT}"
iosMain:     actual fun platformName() = UIDevice.currentDevice.systemName()

Use expect/actual for small stateless platform shims (UUID, current time, logging sink, a Dispatcher choice). Use interfaces for services with state or behavior you want to fake in tests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain
expect fun randomUuid(): String

// androidMain
actual fun randomUuid(): String = java.util.UUID.randomUUID().toString()

// iosMain
import platform.Foundation.NSUUID
actual fun randomUuid(): String = NSUUID().UUIDString()

// Preferred for services:
interface SecureStore { suspend fun put(k: String, v: String); suspend fun get(k: String): String? }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• expect class for a service, then being unable to substitute a fake in common tests.
  • Forgetting that a missing actual in one target fails that target's compilation, not common's.
  • Putting actuals in a different package from the expect.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an actual be in iosMain instead of each iOS target? → Yes, intermediate source sets can host actuals for several targets.
  2. What is @OptionalExpectation? → For expected annotations, platforms that never use them need no actual.
  3. How do you fake an expect fun in a common test? → You cannot swap it; hence wrap it behind an interface at the call site.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE explains the keywords. Senior says the keyword is the last resort, prefers interfaces plus DI, and knows classes are Beta.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An expect object Clock-style singleton made time-dependent code untestable on common targets; replacing it with an injected Clock interface fixed flaky tests.

questions.promptHtml: Explain KMP source sets and the default hierarchy template. Where does code for iosArm64 and iosSimulatorArm64 live?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gradle/KMP structure confusion is the number one onboarding blocker; they want to see you understand visibility of APIs per set.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A source set is a folder of Kotlin plus its dependencies and compiler settings. commonMain sees only APIs available on all targets. Intermediate sets like appleMain and iosMain share code across subsets of targets, and they can use iOS APIs. The Kotlin Gradle plugin's default hierarchy template creates those intermediate sets automatically from the targets you declare, so iOS code goes in iosMain, not per-target folders.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the Kotlin docs, the toolchain limits each source set to APIs available on all targets it compiles to. So commonMain cannot call java.io.File. The default hierarchy template: declare androidTarget() (or the new Android-KMP library plugin), iosArm64(), iosSimulatorArm64() and you get appleMain, nativeMain, iosMain as needed. Accessors are type-safe (iosMain). Explicit dependsOn() calls cancel the template with a warning, so mix manual and default only via applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate(). Opt-out: kotlin.mpp.applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate=false.

commonMain
 ├─ androidMain
 └─ nativeMain
     └─ appleMain
         └─ iosMain
             ├─ iosArm64Main
             └─ iosSimulatorArm64Main

Tests mirror this: commonTest, iosTest, etc. Unsupported sharing combos per docs: multiple JVM targets, JVM+Android, multiple JS targets.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
kotlin {
    androidTarget()
    iosArm64()
    iosSimulatorArm64()
    sourceSets {
        commonMain.dependencies { implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:<version>") }
        iosMain.dependencies { /* iOS-only deps */ }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing val iosMain by creating { dependsOn(commonMain.get()) } on top of the template, which cancels it.
  • Placing iOS code in iosArm64Main only, so the simulator target does not compile.
  • Adding a dependency to commonMain that has no iOS artifact.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why two iOS simulator/device targets? → Different CPU/ABI; Apple silicon sim is arm64, device is arm64, Intel sim needs x64 (verify whether still needed for your team).
  2. Does iosMain have access to UIKit? → Yes, via platform libs.
  3. How do you share between Android and JVM desktop? → A custom jvmCommon intermediate set via manual hierarchy is not template-supported for Android+JVM combos, so avoid it or use a separate module.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists folders. Senior explains the visibility rule, the template/dependsOn conflict and its effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A build broke on CI only for iosSimulatorArm64 because an actual was placed in iosArm64Main.

questions.promptHtml: Name the standard KMP-compatible stack for networking, serialization, persistence and async, and the platform-specific piece each needs.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real KMP work starts with picking libraries that have non-JVM artifacts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Ktor client for HTTP with a per-platform engine (OkHttp on Android, Darwin on iOS), kotlinx.serialization for JSON, kotlinx.coroutines for async, SQLDelight (or Room KMP) for SQL with a per-platform driver, DataStore for key-value, kotlinx-datetime for time, and Koin or kotlin-inject for DI. Retrofit, Gson, Hilt and plain Room-on-JVM are JVM-only and cannot sit in commonMain.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Need KMP choice Platform piece
HTTP Ktor client engine: OkHttp / Darwin
JSON kotlinx.serialization (compiler plugin) none
SQL SQLDelight 2.x or Room KMP (Android, iOS, JVM per Jetpack table; no web) driver: AndroidSqliteDriver / NativeSqliteDriver, or bundled SQLite driver for Room
Prefs Jetpack DataStore (KMP-supported per developer.android.com) file path per platform
Paging AndroidX Paging (KMP table) none
Time kotlinx-datetime none
DI Koin, kotlin-inject none
Jetpack ViewModel/Lifecycle/SavedState also publish KMP artifacts. Selection rule: check the Maven artifact for iosArm64 variants, not the README.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain
val client = HttpClient(engine) { install(ContentNegotiation) { json() } }
// androidMain: HttpClient(OkHttp)   iosMain: HttpClient(Darwin)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using java.time or Gson in common code.
  • Picking Room before checking it lacks web target if you target wasm.
  • Forgetting the serialization compiler plugin (kotlin("plugin.serialization")).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the Ktor engine per platform? → Use each platform's native networking stack (TLS, proxies, ATS).
  2. SQLDelight vs Room KMP? → SQLDelight is SQL-first and codegens typed Kotlin; Room KMP keeps annotation DAO model and Android migration paths.
  3. Does Retrofit work? → No, JVM-only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists libraries. Senior adds drivers/engines, artifact checks, and the migration path from Retrofit/Room.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team discovered a transitive JVM-only dependency only when the first iOS link failed.

questions.promptHtml: Hilt does not work in commonMain. How do you do dependency injection in a KMP codebase, and what are the trade-offs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that Hilt/Dagger rely on JVM annotation processing and Android components, and whether you can design a DI boundary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt is JVM and Android specific, so shared code cannot use it. Options: Koin (runtime service locator DSL, works in common), kotlin-inject (compile-time, KSP-generated, multiplatform), or manual constructor injection with a hand-written composition root. I keep shared classes DI-framework-free with constructor injection, and wire them in one composition root per platform. The Android app can keep Hilt and just provide the shared graph to it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Shared classes take dependencies by constructor and depend on interfaces. Platform pieces (secure store, engine) are provided by the platform. Two common shapes:

shared module:   fun createSharedGraph(platform: PlatformDeps): SharedGraph
androidApp:      Hilt @Provides wraps SharedGraph pieces
iosApp (Swift):  SharedGraph created at app start, passed into views

Koin: simple, no codegen, but errors surface at runtime (missing binding crashes when resolved). kotlin-inject: compile-time graph validation similar in spirit to Dagger, KSP-based; smaller community. Manual DI: zero magic, verbose past ~50 bindings. Hilt on Android + manual graph in shared is a pragmatic split.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain: no framework annotations
class OrdersRepository(private val api: OrdersApi, private val db: OrdersDb)

class SharedGraph(platform: PlatformDeps) {
    private val client = createHttpClient(platform.engineFactory)
    val ordersRepository = OrdersRepository(OrdersApi(client), OrdersDb(platform.sqlDriver))
}

// androidMain: Hilt module exposing it
// @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
// object SharedModule { @Provides @Singleton fun graph(@ApplicationContext c: Context) = SharedGraph(AndroidDeps(c)) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting @Inject or Koin get() calls leak into domain classes (service locator in disguise).
  • Starting Koin twice on Android process recreation.
  • Resolving dependencies from Swift without a stable entry point.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Compile-time vs runtime graph validation? → Koin offers verify() tests; kotlin-inject fails at build time.
  2. How do iOS views get ViewModels? → Via a factory from the shared graph, held by SwiftUI.
  3. Scoping? → Manual: hold instances in the graph; per-screen scope means creating child graphs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use Koin". Senior keeps shared code framework-free and explains the composition-root contract per platform.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Koin missing-binding crash appeared only on a rarely visited iOS screen, fixed by adding a checkModules test to CI.

questions.contextHtml:
A team adds a watchOS target to a shared module. Android builds fine; iOS builds after the change now fail on CI with "Unresolved reference: UIDevice" in iosMain. Gradle output shows w: Declaring a dependsOn relation on a source set cancels the default hierarchy template. This is the build file:

kotlin {
    androidTarget()
    iosArm64(); iosSimulatorArm64(); watchosArm64()
    sourceSets {
        val appleMain by creating { dependsOn(commonMain.get()) }
        iosArm64Main.get().dependsOn(appleMain)
        iosSimulatorArm64Main.get().dependsOn(appleMain)
        watchosArm64Main.get().dependsOn(appleMain)
    }
}

The release is blocked and the dev who wrote it left.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add UIKit as a dependency" or move the code to iosArm64Main. Treats a hierarchy bug as a missing library, and creates duplication.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did it compile before watchOS was added (isolates the change)? Is iosMain code using UIKit-only APIs? Do we really need watchOS now?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the watchOS target and the manual appleMain block to unblock the release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) manual dependsOn cancelled the default template so iosMain no longer exists in the hierarchy as expected; (b) new appleMain is shared with watchOS, which lacks UIKit/UIDevice; (c) missing cinterop; (d) stale Gradle cache (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the warning text; run ./gradlew :shared:tasks and check source set graph in the IDE project structure; compile iosArm64 only vs watchosArm64 only.
  5. Root cause: Declaring dependsOn cancels the template, and the hand-made appleMain now compiles for watchOS, where UIKit APIs are not available. The toolchain restricts a source set to APIs common to all its targets, so UIDevice is unresolved.
  6. Fix: Delete the manual block and rely on the template, which gives appleMain, iosMain, watchosMain correctly; move UIKit code into iosMain, and share only Foundation-level code in appleMain. If an extra set is needed, call applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate() first.
  7. Prevention: CI compiles every declared target (compileKotlin<Target>), review rule against manual dependsOn.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not opt out of the template (kotlin.mpp.applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate=false) just to keep old code; it moves a one-time fix into permanent maintenance.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if you truly need a custom set (e.g. iosAndWatch)? → Call applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate() then add sets; the docs say the template itself cannot be modified.
  • Could expect/actual solve the UIKit gap? → Yes, expect in appleMain, actual per OS set.
  • The Gradle cache was cleared and nothing changed; why? → The cause was model structure, not cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hand-rolled hierarchy copied from a 2021 blog post silently stopped matching the template after an upgrade; the fix was a deletion, and the lesson was "delete config before adding config".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds dependencies or duplicates code per target.
  • Hire: identifies the cancelled template and removes manual dependsOn.
  • Strong hire: explains the all-targets API rule, moves UIKit to iosMain, adds CI per-target compile.

questions.promptHtml: What is the status of Compose Multiplatform per platform, and how would you decide whether to share UI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates repeat stale "CMP iOS is alpha" claims. Seniors know current status and treat it as an adoption decision, not a feature.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compose Multiplatform is JetBrains' UI framework built on Jetpack Compose runtime. Per the sources I read, desktop has been stable since 2023 and iOS reached stable in May 2025 (CMP 1.8.0); web status I would verify on the current compatibility page before committing. Sharing UI is independent of sharing logic: you can use shared logic with native SwiftUI, or share Compose UI fully, or embed Compose screens in a native app.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CMP renders with Skia on iOS (not UIKit widgets), so look-and-feel is Compose's, with interop APIs for hosting UIKit views and embedding Compose inside SwiftUI/UIKit. Jetpack libraries with KMP artifacts (per developer.android.com): lifecycle, viewmodel, navigation, navigation3, savedstate, paging, datastore, with Compose-related ones published by JetBrains for non-Android targets. Android-only pieces (Maps Compose, rxjava adapters) are not in common. Decision factors:

Brand-led, consistent UI, small team  -> share UI
Platform-fidelity critical, large iOS team, heavy native SDKs -> share logic only
Incremental -> embed CMP screens inside native navigation, grow later

Costs to mention: larger iOS binary (verify actual size), accessibility parity, text input/IME quirks, and iOS engineers needing Compose knowledge.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain
@Composable fun OrderScreen(state: OrderState, onRetry: () -> Unit) { /* shared UI */ }

// iosMain: expose to Swift
fun OrderViewController(state: OrderState) = ComposeUIViewController { OrderScreen(state) {} }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting old alpha/beta status.
  • Assuming Android-only Compose APIs (e.g., LocalContext) exist in common.
  • Ignoring that native team skills drive maintainability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you mix? → Yes, ComposeUIViewController embeds in UIKit; SwiftUI interop via UIViewControllerRepresentable.
  2. Performance on iOS? → Skia rendering; measure on your lowest device, do not trust general claims.
  3. Web? → Verify current stability; treat as separate risk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Compose everywhere". Senior frames UI sharing as a staged, reversible decision tied to team skills and accessibility requirements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team shipped CMP screens in a native shell for the checkout flow only, keeping SwiftUI for platform-native chrome.

questions.promptHtml: How does Kotlin code get consumed from Swift, and what gets lost in translation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The ObjC bridge is where KMP pain concentrates.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin/Native exports a framework with an Objective-C header, and Swift sees that header. So Swift sees ObjC-shaped APIs: no Swift generics beyond what ObjC supports, sealed classes become class hierarchies you must cast, enums with associated values do not exist, suspend functions become completion-handler functions, and Flow appears as an opaque type. Tools like SKIE improve this at the Swift level.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mappings: Kotlin Int becomes Int32, Long Int64, List<T> NSArray (no element types in Swift without generics hints), nullable primitives box to NSNumber, suspend fun to completionHandler, default parameters are dropped (no overloads), top-level functions go to a FileNameKt class. Kotlin exceptions: only @Throws-declared ones become NSError; others crash the app on iOS.

Kotlin:  sealed interface UiState { object Loading; data class Data(val items: List<Item>) }
Swift:   UiStateLoading / UiStateData classes, manual `if let` casts, no exhaustive switch (without SKIE)

Fix levers: @ObjCName, @HiddenFromObjC, SKIE (compiler plugin that generates Swift-friendly sealed enums, async/await bridging for suspend and Flow), Swift export (experimental, verify current status).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class AuthRepo {
    @Throws(AuthException::class)   // without this, throwing crashes the iOS process
    suspend fun login(user: String, pass: String): Session = TODO()
}
// Swift, with SKIE / async bridging
let session = try await repo.login(user: u, pass: p)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Missing @Throws on suspend functions, causing hard crashes.
  • Exposing generic collections and getting Any? on the Swift side.
  • Exporting whole transitive dependencies in the framework.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do exceptions crash? → ObjC has no exception model for Kotlin types; uncaught ones terminate.
  2. How to reduce API noise? → internal by default, @HiddenFromObjC, a thin facade.
  3. Swift export? → Direct Swift API generation, experimental per my knowledge; verify.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it is just a framework". Senior designs a deliberate iOS-facing facade and handles errors and nullability explicitly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An iOS-only crash cluster traced to an uncaught Kotlin IOException thrown through a suspend function with no @Throws.

questions.promptHtml: How do you expose a Kotlin StateFlow or suspend function to SwiftUI safely, including cancellation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Concurrency across the language boundary is where leaks and crashes appear.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Raw Flow is unusable from Swift, so I either use SKIE (which turns Flow into AsyncSequence and suspend into async, with cancellation), or KMP-NativeCoroutines, or a hand-written wrapper with collect and a closeable handle. I never use two of those on the same declaration (Touchlab warns against it). The Swift side must cancel the Task when the view disappears.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cancellation chain: SwiftUI .task {} creates a Swift Task; on view disappear it cancels; SKIE propagates that into Kotlin coroutine cancellation. A manual wrapper must return a Cancellable/Closeable that cancels the Kotlin Job.

SwiftUI .task -> Swift Task -> (SKIE) -> Kotlin collect -> StateFlow
   cancel on disappear ------------------------------> Job.cancel()

Threading: Kotlin/Native allows any thread now (new memory manager), but UI updates must be dispatched to main; Kotlin Dispatchers.Main on iOS uses the main dispatch queue. State holders should expose StateFlow, not SharedFlow of events (lost events).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// manual wrapper fallback
class FlowHandle(private val job: Job) { fun cancel() = job.cancel() }
fun <T> Flow<T>.watch(scope: CoroutineScope, onEach: (T) -> Unit): FlowHandle =
    FlowHandle(onEach { onEach(it) }.launchIn(scope))
.task { for await s in vm.state { self.ui = s } }  // SKIE; cancelled with the view

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Collecting in init of an ObservableObject and never cancelling (leak).
  • Using Dispatchers.Default collectors that mutate SwiftUI state off main.
  • Mixing SKIE and NativeCoroutines on the same API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why StateFlow over SharedFlow? → Replays latest, safe for re-subscription after view reappears.
  2. How to run Kotlin scope lifecycle on iOS? → Shared ViewModel from Jetpack lifecycle KMP, cleared via viewModelScope when holder released (verify iOS clear semantics).
  3. How to test? → Test shared logic in common with Turbine; keep Swift layer thin.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use a callback". Senior ties Swift Task cancellation to Job cancellation and picks one bridging strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen kept collecting after pop, doubling network refreshes.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the Kotlin/Native memory manager and its interaction with Swift ARC. What leaks can still happen?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The old freezing model is gone; seniors know the modern one and the cross-heap retain cycles that remain.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin/Native has a tracing GC (concurrent mark and sweep, non-generational per the docs), with a shared heap accessible from any thread, so the old frozen-object restrictions are gone. Swift uses ARC. Kotlin objects referenced from Swift are retained via stable references, and Swift objects referenced from Kotlin are retained by ARC. A cycle across the two heaps (Kotlin lambda holding a Swift view model that holds the Kotlin object) is not collected by either collector, so you must break such cycles.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GC triggers by memory pressure heuristics or timer; marking is parallel and concurrent; stop-the-world only if allocation outpaces GC. Tuning flags in gradle.properties: kotlin.native.binary.gc=pmcs (alternative collector), kotlin.native.binary.gcMarkSingleThreaded=true, -Xruntime-logs=gc=info, Instruments signposts via kotlin.native.binary.enableSafepointSignposts=true. kotlin.native.binary.pagedAllocator=false reduces memory under strict limits; Latin-1 strings flag is experimental.

Swift VC --strong--> Kotlin ViewModel --lambda--> Swift closure --strong--> VC
   ARC cannot see through Kotlin heap; GC cannot see Swift's refcount => leak

Fix with weak captures in Swift closures and explicit close()/cancel when the screen goes away.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
vm.onEvent = { [weak self] e in self?.handle(e) }   // break the cross-heap cycle
// test for leaks using GC.lastGCInfo (see docs) after GC.collect()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming "freeze()" is still required.
  • Assuming GC will clean cross-language cycles.
  • Large caches in singletons inflating iOS memory with no pressure signal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to observe GC pauses? → Safepoint signposts in Instruments.
  2. Does unused memory return to the OS? → Allocator behavior varies; verify on your Kotlin version.
  3. Background threads touching objects? → Allowed now, but still need synchronization for mutable state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "no more freezing". Senior explains the two-collector cycle problem and the diagnostics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen retained its view model forever because of a callback pair across Swift and Kotlin.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (1.2M DAU, 55 percent iOS) shares its data layer via KMP. After release 4.18, iOS crash-free sessions drop from 99.7 to 98.9 percent. Crash reports show Uncaught Kotlin exception: kotlinx.io.IOException: Connection reset plus kfun:kotlin.Throwable#... on the main thread. Android is unaffected. Memory graphs also show iOS resident memory climbing 120 MB over 20 minutes on the transactions screen. A prior release changed the refresh() function from regular to suspend.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and say what you would change in process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/catch around the network call" without understanding why iOS and not Android, and ignoring the memory trend as unrelated.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do crashes correlate with flaky networks? Is refresh called from Swift directly? Did the memory climb exist before 4.18? Any SKIE or bridging library upgrade?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side flag to stop auto-refresh on the screen, or hotfix with an Android-parity catch in the shared repository, and halt staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Kotlin exception propagating through a suspend function lacking @Throws; (b) Flow collected on screen never cancelled (explains memory); (c) cross-heap retain cycle; (d) new Kotlin version GC behavior (red herring until checked).
  4. How I'd verify each: Symbolicate crash with dSYM, inspect header for @Throws; Xcode Memory Graph for retained Kotlin objects; Instruments Allocations; GC logs (-Xruntime-logs=gc=info).
  5. Root cause: refresh became suspend without @Throws; a network IOException escaped to ObjC, which has no handler, crashing the process. Separately the SwiftUI view model started collecting a flow in init without cancel, accumulating collectors.
  6. Fix: Short term: catch and map to a Result in shared code. Long term: policy that every public suspend function in the iOS facade returns a sealed result or is annotated @Throws, and use SKIE or structured .task collection.
  7. Prevention: a lint/Konsist rule requiring @Throws on public suspend functions in the facade, an iOS UI test with network disconnection, crash-free gating in staged rollout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blanket-catch Throwable (swallows CancellationException and hides bugs), and would not disable GC flags to "fix" memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the crash is only on iOS 16? → Check the OS network stack difference and Darwin engine behavior; reproduce with network link conditioner.
  • Can a suspending function cancel safely from Swift? → Yes with SKIE async bridging; otherwise manual.
  • Why did Android not crash? → JVM uncaught exceptions are handled by the app's own handler or propagate normally in coroutines scope.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team turned every repository function into Result at the boundary after a two-week crash chase; Swift code became simpler and the crash class disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network or iOS and wraps with try/catch only.
  • Hire: finds the missing @Throws and the leak.
  • Strong hire: adds boundary Result policy, lint, rollout gating, and explains CancellationException handling.

questions.promptHtml: How would you structure a shared KMP module so Android and iOS both consume it cleanly? Where does the ViewModel live?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests architectural layering plus knowing what the platform boundary should expose.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I split shared code into data (Ktor, SQLDelight, repositories), domain (use cases, models), and presentation (state holders exposing StateFlow<UiState> plus intent functions). Android and iOS UIs only render state and send intents. Presentation can use Jetpack ViewModel, which now has KMP artifacts, or a plain class with its own scope. The iOS-facing surface is a small facade, not the whole module.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
:app-android (Compose/XML)     iosApp (SwiftUI)
        \                        /
         :shared:presentation (StateFlow<UiState>, onIntent)
         :shared:domain
         :shared:data  --> platform drivers/engines via interfaces

Multi-module vs single: one umbrella framework for iOS (an XCFramework re-exporting modules) because each separate Kotlin framework duplicates the Kotlin runtime and stdlib, bloating the app. So Gradle sub-modules are fine, but the iOS-exported framework should be one umbrella with explicit export() of only the public API. Keep internal visibility default to shrink the ObjC surface. Unidirectional data flow (see the architecture chunks) applies unchanged; only the collection mechanism differs on iOS.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class OrdersViewModel(private val repo: OrdersRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<OrdersUi>(OrdersUi.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<OrdersUi> = _state
    fun onIntent(i: OrdersIntent) { /* viewModelScope.launch { ... } */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One Kotlin framework per module, duplicating runtime.
  • Exposing Flow<List<Entity>> with DB types to Swift.
  • Putting navigation in the shared layer without a clear contract.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not share the ViewModel? → You can, via Jetpack lifecycle KMP; iOS must hold and clear it deliberately.
  2. Navigation? → Usually native per platform; shared emits navigation intents/effects.
  3. How to version public API? → Treat the facade like a library; binary-compatibility checks (e.g., a validator plugin, verify).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE draws layers. Senior addresses the umbrella-framework runtime duplication and facade/export hygiene.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Splitting into three frameworks added about 18 MB to the iOS IPA (illustrative) until consolidated.

questions.contextHtml: A 9-year-old Android app (2.3M DAU, 400k lines Kotlin, Hilt, Retrofit, Room) and a Swift iOS app have drifting business rules: a refund-eligibility bug fixed on Android 3 weeks earlier still exists on iOS (cost: 1,100 support tickets). Leadership asks for "KMP for all shared logic in two quarters". Two iOS devs have never touched Kotlin. Releases are weekly, with staged rollout.
questions.promptHtml: How do you introduce KMP without a freeze or a big-bang rewrite?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Create a shared module and move everything" or "rewrite networking in Ktor first". High risk, no value until done.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which rules cause the most defects? Do iOS devs have CI Mac capacity? Who owns the shared module? What is the appetite for binary size (+MB)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the refund bug on iOS now natively; do not wait for KMP.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The risk is organizational more than technical: (a) iOS adoption friction, (b) build time growth, (c) binary size, (d) Hilt/Room friction on Android side.
  4. How I'd verify each: A 2-week spike moving only RefundEligibility (pure Kotlin, no dependencies) into a new shared module; measure clean and incremental build time, IPA size delta, and developer feedback.
  5. Root cause: Duplicate implementations of rules is a process problem; shared code removes the second implementation.
  6. Fix: Phase 1 pure-logic leaf modules (rules, validators, mappers) behind interfaces, with golden test vectors run on both platforms. Phase 2 data layer (Ktor/SQLDelight) feature by feature behind existing repository interfaces so Android keeps Retrofit meanwhile. Phase 3 evaluate shared presentation. Each phase behind a remote flag with ability to fall back to the native implementation (run both and compare in shadow mode first).
  7. Prevention: Joint ownership and a shared contract test suite; Konsist rules about layer dependencies; track defect-parity metrics.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No rewrite of persistence early, no sharing UI in phase 1, no deadline-driven percentage targets.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• iOS team refuses Kotlin? → Ship the framework as a binary dependency and pair on debugging; show defect reduction.
  • Build time up 6 minutes? → Binary caching, build only the iosSimulatorArm64 slice in dev, XCFramework prebuilt for iOS devs.
  • Rollback? → Remote flag falls back to the native implementation for one release cycle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Shadow-mode comparison of the shared rule against the legacy iOS logic found 0.4 percent disagreement, which exposed three legacy bugs before the switch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite.
  • Hire: incremental leaf-module plan with measurement.
  • Strong hire: shadow mode, flagged fallback, ownership/process plan and cost metrics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test shared KMP code, including expect/actual and platform-specific behavior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Confirms you know the test source sets, the fake strategy, and the cost of platform parity bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I write most tests in commonTest with kotlin.test, coroutines-test and Turbine, using fakes for platform interfaces. Platform-specific actuals get tests in androidUnitTest or iosTest. CI runs the common tests on JVM/Android and on iOS simulator (iosSimulatorArm64Test), because Kotlin/Native behavior (e.g., string formatting, collections ordering, date handling) can differ from JVM.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key gotcha: tests that pass on JVM can fail on K/N. Run the same commonTest on both. Main dispatcher: no main loop in K/N tests, so use Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher). Contract tests: write an abstract test class for an interface and run it against each platform implementation.

commonTest   -> fakes, logic, flows          (runs on every target)
androidUnitTest / iosTest -> real actuals    (platform specific)
UI tests     -> native (Espresso/XCUITest) or Compose UI tests

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class RefundTest {
    @Test fun goldTierGetsDiscount() = runTest {
        assertEquals(90, DiscountPolicy().apply(100, Tier.GOLD))
    }
}
abstract class SecureStoreContract { abstract fun create(): SecureStore
    @Test fun roundTrip() = runTest { val s = create(); s.put("k","v"); assertEquals("v", s.get("k")) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only running tests on JVM.
  • Using real Dispatchers.Main.
  • Tests that rely on default locale/timezone.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to run iOS tests on CI? → macOS runners with ./gradlew iosSimulatorArm64Test.
  2. Mocking library? → Mockk is JVM-only; use fakes or a KMP mocking library (verify).
  3. Flow testing? → Turbine.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes unit tests. Senior builds contract tests per interface and runs on native targets.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A date formatting test passed on JVM, failed on iOS due to locale default differences, and was caught only on the iOS CI leg.

questions.contextHtml: A shared KMP module builds Android + iOS. Developers complain: clean CI build is 38 minutes (was 14 before adding iOS), incremental iOS builds take 7-9 minutes after touching a single common file. Xcode warns about duplicated Kotlin runtime symbols in the app because two frameworks (Core.framework, Features.framework) are embedded. CI Mac runners cost $0.08 per minute, 220 PR builds per week.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy faster machines" or "enable Gradle caching" without finding where the time goes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 38 minutes link time or compile time? Are we building release (LTO-style full) or debug frameworks on PRs? How many iOS targets are built per PR?
  2. Immediate mitigation: PRs build only iosSimulatorArm64 debug; device and release builds run on merge/nightly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) building all iOS targets and release frameworks on every PR; (b) two frameworks relinking everything; (c) no remote build cache; (d) Kotlin daemon memory pressure (verify with scan); (e) cinterop regeneration.
  4. How I'd verify each: ./gradlew --scan, check task timeline for link*Framework*; --profile; compare debug vs release link time; check org.gradle.caching hit rates.
  5. Root cause: Release-mode native linking and two frameworks each linking the full module graph; PRs built every target.
  6. Fix: One umbrella framework (export() only what Swift needs); debug build type on PRs; enable Gradle remote build cache and configuration cache; tune kotlin.daemon.jvmargs/org.gradle.jvmargs; use embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode for Xcode integration so only the active architecture builds.
  7. Prevention: Build-time budget in CI and a weekly scan trend; Gradle --scan links stored on PRs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not splitting the iOS app into per-feature frameworks (runtime duplication); not removing release linking from the merge pipeline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cache hit rate low on iOS? → Check task inputs including absolute paths and Xcode env variables.
  • Use XCFramework everywhere? → Only for distribution; local dev uses the Xcode run-script task.
  • Cost? → Previous: 220 x 38 min x $0.08 = $668.8/week; target 220 x 15 x 0.08 = $264.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving PR builds to the simulator arch alone cut weekly CI spend by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: generic "more cache".
  • Hire: finds link tasks, builds fewer targets.
  • Strong hire: umbrella framework, build scan evidence, cost math.

questions.promptHtml: What are the most common Gradle and project-setup pitfalls in a KMP project, and how do you avoid them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior will be the person debugging the build for the team.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Version mismatch between Kotlin, Compose Multiplatform compiler plugin, KSP and AGP; the Android plugin choice (the androidTarget() DSL vs the newer Android-KMP library plugin that Android Studio's module wizard applies); manual hierarchy breaking the template; transitive dependencies without iOS artifacts; Xcode integration scripts; and multiple frameworks duplicating the runtime. I use version catalogs, one Kotlin version across modules, and CI that compiles every target.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compatibility: KSP versions are tied to the Kotlin version (since KSP2, verify for your Kotlin), Compose Multiplatform has its own compatibility table; check it before bumping Kotlin.
  • Android plugin: with newer AGP, the dedicated Android-KMP library plugin replaces com.android.library inside KMP modules (verify the minimum AGP and its limitations such as variants and Java sources).
  • Xcode: integration through the embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode Gradle task from a build phase script; wrong FRAMEWORK_SEARCH_PATHS and sandboxing of user scripts are classic breakers.
  • Dependency export: only api + export() types visible to Swift.
  • gradle.properties flags such as kotlin.native.ignoreDisabledTargets, memory (verify) for Mac vs Linux CI.
Linux CI: can compile Android/JVM; iOS targets need macOS (cannot build Apple targets on Linux)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
kotlin {
    listOf(iosArm64(), iosSimulatorArm64()).forEach {
        it.binaries.framework { baseName = "Shared"; isStatic = true }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dynamic frameworks used by default where static is simpler for Xcode embedding.
  • Upgrading Kotlin without checking Compose/KSP compatibility.
  • Gradle daemon out of memory on native link.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Linux CI not enough? → Apple targets need Xcode toolchain.
  2. Static vs dynamic framework? → Static usually avoids embedding/signing issues; a dynamic one can be needed for multi-framework setups (verify).
  3. Version catalog use? → One source of truth for the Kotlin and plugin versions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the Gradle DSL. Senior knows the failure modes and the CI matrix that catches them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin minor bump broke the Compose compiler pairing and blocked releases for two days.

questions.contextHtml: A 14-person mobile team (8 Android, 6 iOS) is deciding on KMP. The iOS lead is skeptical: "We will own Kotlin crashes in an app we cannot debug." Product wants a 30 percent faster feature delivery. App: 600k DAU, feature parity gaps cost two sprints per quarter. Budget allows no new headcount.
questions.promptHtml: What do you propose, and how do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mandates KMP from the top, or accepts the iOS lead's "no" without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the top three parity defects? What are the iOS team's actual concerns (debugging, tooling, hiring, binary size)? What is the exit cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None required; this is a decision, not an incident. Reduce parity cost with shared specs/contract tests meanwhile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Real concern is debuggability and ownership; (b) CI/build cost; (c) hiring; (d) vendor/tool maturity.
  4. How I'd verify each: A time-boxed pilot (6 weeks) on one non-critical domain with iOS dev as co-owner; measure defects, lead time, build time, binary size; test LLDB debugging and crash symbolication.
  5. Root cause: Sharing is a socio-technical change; the iOS team must be a first-class owner of shared code.
  6. Fix: Joint ownership rotation, iOS devs reviewing shared PRs, crash tooling for K/N symbolication set up before launch, explicit exit plan (the pilot module can be reimplemented natively).
  7. Prevention: Decision record with success metrics and a re-evaluation date.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No mandate, no UI sharing as part of the pilot, no comparison on "lines shared" alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pilot succeeds technically but iOS devs dislike it? → Weight their feedback; continue only if maintenance cost is acceptable.
  • New hires? → Kotlin skill pool vs Swift; both platforms' job profiles shift.
  • Executive wants Flutter instead? → See the KMP vs Flutter comparison questions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The skeptic became the owner of the shared networking module after he found he could ship fixes once instead of twice.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: opinion without data.
  • Hire: pilot with metrics.
  • Strong hire: ownership model, exit plan, and tooling readiness.

questions.promptHtml: Common Kotlin code compiles for both targets, yet behaves differently on iOS than on Android in places. Which differences bite, and how do you design around them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "It is the same Kotlin" is the junior assumption. Seniors know where semantics, performance, and APIs diverge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The language is shared, but the runtime and platform are not. Differences I plan for: text and locale (formatting, collation, case mapping), time zone and date APIs, threading and the main dispatcher in tests, exceptions crossing into Swift, memory and GC characteristics, reflection (limited on Native), and library availability. I isolate these behind small interfaces, pin locale and zone in tests, and run common tests on both targets.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• No reflection-based tooling in common code: serialization uses compiler plugins, not runtime reflection.
  • String.format-style and locale-aware functions are not in the common stdlib in the same form; use kotlinx-datetime and an explicit formatter interface when output must match.
  • Number formatting and sorting rely on platform locale if done through platform APIs; golden-file tests will differ per OS.
  • Threads: Dispatchers.Main exists on iOS but has no loop in plain Native tests (see Q312).
  • Exceptions: uncaught Kotlin exceptions on iOS crash unless @Throws (Q306).
  • Performance: K/N GC differs from ART; allocation-heavy loops need measuring on both.
Rule: if user-visible output depends on locale/time zone, test it on both targets with fixed inputs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface MoneyFormatter { fun format(paise: Long, localeTag: String): String }
// androidMain: java.text.NumberFormat; iosMain: NSNumberFormatter
// commonTest: contract test with fixed locale and expected strings per platform

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asserting locale-formatted strings in common tests that run on both.
  • Assuming hashCode/iteration order are identical across targets for unordered collections.
  • Relying on JVM-only features (synchronized, Thread) via leaked JVM habits (use coroutines Mutex / atomics).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to handle time zones? → Inject a TimeZone/Clock, test with fixed zones.
  2. Can you use synchronized? → Not in common; use Mutex or kotlinx.atomicfu.
  3. How do you find these bugs early? → Run commonTest on iosSimulatorArm64 in CI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "same language, same behavior". Senior lists divergence classes and isolates them behind contract-tested interfaces.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An invoice screen showed different rounding in INR on iOS versus Android after a locale-dependent formatter was used in shared code.

questions.contextHtml: A Series B startup (3 Android, 2 iOS engineers, one web dev who knows React) is rebuilding its consumer app: 150k MAU target to 1M in 18 months, heavy on animated feed, maps, in-app payments SDKs, push, and camera scanning. The CEO has read that Flutter or React Native could "halve the team". Existing Android app is Kotlin; iOS app is Swift; both are 5 years old and fragile.
questions.promptHtml: Choose between KMP (native UI), KMP with Compose Multiplatform, Flutter, and React Native. Defend it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks by hype or by the engineer's favorite language; ignores native SDK needs and the existing codebase.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What differentiates the product (UI polish vs native capability)? What is the hiring market locally? Is a web app also planned? How strict are accessibility and platform-fidelity requirements? Time-to-market deadline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; the decision must be evidence-driven, not rushed. I would timebox a 2-week spike.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Native-heavy features (maps, payments, camera) favor native UI + KMP logic; (b) tiny team and a web dev favor React Native or Flutter; (c) existing Kotlin/Swift expertise favors KMP; (d) CMP maturity risk on iOS (stable per JetBrains-related sources I read, May 2025; verify).
  4. How I'd verify each: Build the riskiest screen (animated feed + map) in the top two candidates; measure frame times on a low-end Android device and iPhone SE-class device, binary size, dev velocity, native SDK integration effort, accessibility tests.
  5. Root cause: The real question is which cost dominates: duplicated feature work, or integration friction with native SDKs.
  6. Fix (recommendation): With 5 native engineers and SDK-heavy features, I would pick KMP for shared logic with native UI, and evaluate Compose Multiplatform for a few screens later. If the team were 2 engineers, UI-first, I would lean Flutter or React Native. Data point: adoption surveys conflict (sources I found were vendor-written and directional, so I would not cite percentages).
  7. Prevention: Write a decision record with revisit date and kill criteria (e.g., spike frame time > 16 ms p95 on target device).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No rewrite for "team halving" claims; no choice without a vertical-slice spike.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CEO insists on Flutter? → Run the same spike on it with agreed metrics; the data decides, and I would state the migration cost off native SDKs.
  • What if web is required? → React Native/React or Flutter web (verify) or CMP web (verify status).
  • Hiring? → Check local pool for Kotlin/Swift vs Dart/RN.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A vertical-slice spike showed map and payment SDK glue consumed 40 percent of the cross-platform estimate, shifting the decision.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tool preference.
  • Hire: criteria and spike.
  • Strong hire: quantified spike criteria, skills and SDK analysis, reversibility.

questions.promptHtml: Fundamentally, how does KMP differ from Flutter and React Native, and when does each win?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must explain architecture differences, not slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flutter ships its own engine and renders every pixel itself, in Dart. React Native runs JavaScript and maps to native views; since 0.76 (Oct 2024) the New Architecture (Fabric, TurboModules, JSI) is default. KMP compiles Kotlin to native for each platform with no runtime bridge, and shares whatever layer you choose, including optional UI via Compose Multiplatform. KMP wins when you have native teams and need native SDKs and fidelity. Flutter and RN win when one team ships UI quickly on both platforms from scratch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
KMP Flutter React Native
Language Kotlin Dart TypeScript/JS
UI native or Compose MP own renderer native views
Sharing unit any layer nearly everything nearly everything
Native SDK access direct platform channels native modules/JSI
Incremental adoption very easy possible (add-to-app) possible (brownfield)
Biggest risk iOS interop friction, build time non-native look/behavior, Dart pool bridge/JS perf, upgrade churn
Adoption data in sources was conflicting and vendor-biased; treat as directional.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// KMP calls the platform directly, no channel serialization
actual fun openSettings() { UIApplication.sharedApplication.openURL(NSURL(string = UIApplicationOpenSettingsURLString)!!) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming one is "faster" without a workload.
  • Forgetting incremental adoption is KMP's main strength.
  • Comparing only first release, not 3-year maintenance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can Flutter use Kotlin? → Via platform channels only.
  2. Is CMP the same as Flutter? → Similar idea (own rendering on iOS via Skia), but built on Kotlin and Compose and mixable with native UI.
  3. Hiring? → Kotlin/Android developers transition faster to KMP.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives pros/cons list. Senior compares rendering, sharing unit, SDK access, and migration path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Several companies kept native UI and shared logic with KMP to avoid fidelity regressions (public case studies exist, verify specifics before citing).

questions.contextHtml: Your VP says: "Make KMP share at least 80 percent of the code by the end of the year." The app has 520k lines: 38 percent UI, 22 percent platform integrations (push, payments, camera), 40 percent logic. Iosteam is 4 devs. Crash-free sessions are 99.2 percent; the biggest pain is feature delay (parity gaps).
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the number and starts moving UI and platform code to hit it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What outcome is the 80 percent a proxy for (speed, cost, parity)? Measured how (lines, features, modules)? What do we accept as regressions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Propose replacing the metric with outcome metrics: parity-gap lead time, duplicate defect count, release cadence.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The goal is delivery speed; (b) pressure from cost; (c) a competitor claim. Arithmetic check: the logic share is 40 percent, so 80 percent would need nearly all UI shared too.
  4. How I'd verify each: Baseline current parity defects/lead time; estimate what sharing logic alone yields (up to 40 percent by lines) and UI via CMP adds up to 38 percent, leaving 22 percent platform-bound.
  5. Root cause: Percentage is a vanity metric: lines of UI are cheap to write but costly to share; defect parity is driven by logic.
  6. Fix: Offer a plan: logic first (target maybe 60-70 percent of shareable logic), UI sharing for selected flows, platform integrations stay native; report outcome metrics quarterly.
  7. Prevention: Written decision record, quarterly review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not forcing platform integrations into common code via heavy expect/actual; not optimizing a line count.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• VP insists on the number? → Define the denominator (shareable code only) and agree on it in writing.
  • Could 80 percent be reached? → Only with CMP covering most UI, a bigger bet that needs the UI-sharing spike.
  • What do you report? → Lead time, escaped parity defects, build time, binary size.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching the KPI from "percent shared" to "parity defects per release" redirected effort to the 15 percent of code that caused 70 percent of the divergence.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts target blindly.
  • Hire: questions the metric and shows arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: replaces with outcome metrics and a staged plan.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. A shared TokenRefresher used a Mutex and a Clock provided via expect/actual (expect object SystemClock). Last Tuesday 4 percent of iOS users (about 18,000 of 450k DAU) were logged out within an hour; Android was fine. Timeline: backend moved token expiry from 60 to 30 minutes at 09:00. Shared unit tests (JVM only) were green. The iOS actual computed expiry with NSDate().timeIntervalSince1970 in seconds while the common code expected milliseconds.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: causes, contributing factors, and action items.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The developer wrote the wrong unit." Blames a person, no systemic findings.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why only 4 percent (those with sessions longer than 30 min)? Were iOS tests run in CI? Was the backend change communicated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix actual to return milliseconds, expedited release plus server tolerance window; force-refresh token on app start.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) iOS actual unit mismatch (confirmed by reading the actual); (b) backend change exposing it (trigger, not cause); (c) clock skew (red herring); (d) Mutex deadlock (red herring, no hang symptoms).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce in iosSimulatorArm64Test with a fake time; log token expiry deltas; compare auth logs per platform.
  5. Root cause: An unchecked unit contract in an expect/actual boundary, plus tests that run only on JVM, so the iOS actual was never executed in CI. The 30-minute expiry made the latent bug visible.
  6. Fix: Replace expect object with an injected Clock interface (or kotlinx-datetime Clock), define time as Instant not raw numbers, and add a contract test run on every target.
  7. Prevention: CI runs commonTest on iOS simulator; actuals require tests; review checklist for expect/actual units; alert on per-platform forced-logout rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No blame; no removing the Mutex; no "just add a code comment".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not catch it with Android tests? → Android used a different actual.
  • Could types have prevented it? → Yes: Instant/Duration instead of raw Long.
  • How to detect earlier in prod? → Per-platform logout-rate alarm with a 1 percent threshold.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a similar incident, "no raw epoch numbers across module boundaries" became a Konsist check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names the typo as cause.
  • Hire: finds missing iOS test coverage and replaces expect object.
  • Strong hire: typed time, per-platform tests, alerting, blameless action items with owners.
